_comment: Seccomp profile for the code-execution sandbox.
Docker applies a profile to EVERY process in the container, which is the
constraint that shapes everything here: the runner is itself a web server,
so a filter cannot distinguish it from a pupil's program.
The first version of this file denied socket, connect, sendto, recvfrom,
bind, listen and accept. It was never referenced by any compose file, and
wiring it up as written killed the service outright:
ERROR: could not bind on any address out of [('0.0.0.0', 8001)]
uvicorn needs socket, bind, listen and accept to serve at all. So those are
allowed, and the one thing the service never does is denied instead:
connect  - the runner accepts connections and initiates none. A pupil's
program needs this to reach anything, including our own API on
the shared sandbox-net, which is the route this exists to
close. internal: true already closes the internet.
sendto is NOT denied, though it is the obvious second entry. On x86-64
Linux there is no separate send() syscall: glibc implements send() as
sendto(fd, buf, len, flags, NULL, 0). Denying it stopped the server
writing any response at all — uvicorn accepted the request, logged
'200 OK', and the caller saw an empty reply. Measured, and it looks
exactly like a healthy service from the log side.
That leaves a connectionless path — socket(SOCK_DGRAM) then sendto(addr)
— open. It reaches nothing: internal: true closes the internet, and the
only thing on sandbox-net is the backend, which speaks TCP.
What this deliberately does NOT claim: a pupil's program can still create a
socket and listen on one. On an egress-isolated network with nothing
dialling in, that reaches nobody. Denying bind as well would deny it to
uvicorn too, and a sandbox that cannot serve is not a safer sandbox.
Every supported language is run under this profile before it ships; a
syscall filter that breaks a runtime breaks it silently, and only for
whoever happens to use that language.
